strengths: Clear problem formulation: Decoupling high-level spatial visual reasoning from embodiment-specific low-level control using mid-level visual aids (affordance bounding boxes, points, and 2D visual traces) provides an effective inductive bias against embodiment heterogeneity and dataset scarcity.

Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation: The authors evaluate FSD extensively across five general spatial reasoning benchmarks, two free space/object reference benchmarks, a dedicated newly proposed benchmark (VABench), SimplerEnv simulation, and real-world tabletop experiments on an xArm 6 manipulator.

Well-structured data generation and training pipeline: The five-level weak-to-strong capability construction combining large-scale embodied datasets (BridgeData, DROID, RT-X) with 3D spatial relationship grounding and self-consistency alignment is logical and well-engineered.

Solid ablations: The ablation study on VABench clearly quantifies the individual gains brought by both the Spatial Relationship-Focused Chain-of-Thought (SrCoT) and the bidirectional self-consistency alignment mechanism.
weaknesses: Comparison setup nuance in robot execution: In SimplerEnv and real-world experiments, FSD generates 2D traces/affordances which are mapped into 3D via depth cameras and executed with classical motion planners (e.g., GraspNet and CuRobo), whereas several baseline models (e.g., OpenVLA, Octo, RT-1-X) operate purely end-to-end to predict low-level joint/gripper commands. While visual-aid modularity is a legitimate design choice, the advantages of using off-the-shelf collision-free planners vs. end-to-end control should be discussed more critically to ensure fair attribution of performance gains.

Open-loop execution and dynamics: Generating a 2D trace on the initial frame followed by open-loop trajectory tracking can be fragile in dynamic settings or under contact uncertainties (e.g., slipping, unexpected collisions). The paper mentions replanning from intermediate steps, but does not provide an empirical analysis of closed-loop reactivity or latency.

Benchmark scale and qualitative metrics: VABench consists of 300 manually annotated samples, which is somewhat small for a comprehensive evaluation benchmark. Furthermore, relying on 'GPT Score' for qualitative trajectory evaluation introduces potential LLM evaluation bias.

Minor presentation issues: There are minor typographical errors and duplications in the text (e.g., 'Table Table 3b' on page 8, and 'even outperforming VLA models that even outperforming specially fine-tuned VLA models' on page 9).

strengths: Addresses a fundamental challenge in generalist robotic manipulation: overcoming embodiment heterogeneity and dataset scarcity by formulating an embodiment-agnostic mid-level representation (affordance bounding boxes, points, and visual traces) via reasoning rather than pure end-to-end regression.

The proposed Spatial Relationship-Focused Visual Chain-of-Thought (SrCoT) and bidirectional self-consistency alignment provide a structured, principled mechanism for spatial reasoning in VLMs. Ablation studies on VABench cleanly validate the individual impact of SrCoT and alignment.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple axes: 5 general spatial reasoning benchmarks (CVBench, CRPE, SAT, BLINK, EmbSpatial-Bench), 2 reference benchmarks (RoboRefIt, Where2Place), the proposed VABench, SimplerEnv simulation, and physical robot experiments on an xArm 6.

Strong empirical performance: FSD matches or outperforms specialized open-source models across spatial benchmarks and significantly outperforms baselines in both simulation (54.1% average success in SimplerEnv) and real-world tabletop tasks (72% success rate).
weaknesses: Fairness of comparison in the robotics experiments: In Table 4, FSD is evaluated against end-to-end VLA models (Octo, OpenVLA, SpatialVLA) that predict low-level control actions directly from RGB observations. In contrast, FSD predicts 2D traces/affordances, unprojects them to 3D using depth sensor readings, and executes them via an external grasp generator (GraspNet) and trajectory planner (CuRobo). This introduces an asymmetry in inputs (access to depth sensing and collision-aware motion planning) that is not fully controlled for in the comparison.

Open-loop execution limitations: The execution framework relies on back-projecting 2D waypoints using single-view/preliminary depth and executing interpolated trajectories in SE(3). The paper does not thoroughly discuss how the system handles runtime dynamic obstacles, non-rigid object deformation (e.g., in cloth folding), or execution failures that require reactive visual closed-loop feedback.

Baselines on VABench: For visual trace evaluation (VABench-VisualTrace), the only compared baseline is an internal DINOv2 Predictor baseline. Comparisons against existing visual-trace prediction methods (e.g., LLaRVA or Track2Act) are missing.

Presentation and writing polish: Several minor inconsistencies and drafting artifacts appear throughout the manuscript. For instance, in Figure 1 under the 'Projection' block, placeholder text ('balabal a') remains; the real-world success rate is cited inconsistently as 72% in the abstract and conclusion vs. 73% in Section 1; and Table 3 is referred to redundantly as 'Table Table 3b' in Section 6.1.

Key experimental details deferred to the appendix: Crucial setup details, such as the exact number of trials per task and specific success criteria for the 8 real-world robot tasks, are omitted from the main text.

strengths: Broad evaluation across vision-language benchmarks: The paper evaluates the model across 8 existing benchmarks covering general spatial reasoning (CVBench, SAT, BLINK, CRPE, EmbSpatial-Bench) and embodied reference (RoboRefIt, Where2Place), showing competitive results among open-source 13B models.

Well-structured data generation pipeline: The hierarchical 5-level pipeline for generating spatial relations, affordance boxes/points, and trajectories from robotic datasets (BridgeDataV2, RT-X, DROID) using vision foundation models (Metric3Dv2, Grounded-SAM, CoTracker) is systematically designed.

Bidirectional self-consistency alignment: Inverting visual aid generation into an instruction prediction task is a sensible auxiliary training objective to bridge coordinate tokens and textual instruction semantics.
weaknesses: Unfair and confounding comparison with VLA baselines: The comparison between FSD and end-to-end VLA models (Octo, OpenVLA, SpatialVLA) in Table 4 and real-world experiments is fundamentally mismatched. FSD only outputs 2D image coordinates/trajectories, which are then lifted to 3D using calibrated depth cameras, grasped via GraspNet, and executed using an advanced collision-free motion planner (CuRobo). In contrast, end-to-end VLAs directly predict low-level control actions from RGB inputs without privileged depth sensors or trajectory optimization. Attributing the 30%+ performance gain entirely to FSD's spatial reasoning is methodologically flawed.

Limited baseline comparisons on visual aid generation: On the proposed VABench-VisualTrace benchmark, FSD is only compared against an ad-hoc baseline ('DINOv2 Predictor') trained by the authors. Crucial existing models that predict visual traces or point flows for manipulation (such as LLaRVA, Track2Act, or Flow-based policies) are omitted from the trajectory evaluation.

Limited conceptual novelty: Structuring manipulation via intermediate visual representations (affordance points, boxes, and visual trajectories) has been extensively explored in recent literature (e.g., RoboPoint, Where2Act, LLaRVA, ReKep). Furthermore, the Spatial Relationship-Focused Visual Chain-of-Thought (SrCoT) relies on rigid, templated reasoning formats rather than emergent reasoning.

Insufficient real-robot evaluation statistics: The real-world evaluation in Section 6.2 and Figure 7 does not specify the number of trials per task in the main text. The resulting discrete success rate increments (e.g., 20%, 40%, 60%, 80%) suggest a very small sample size (likely 5 trials per task), which lacks statistical significance for robotic manipulation claims.

2D-to-3D projection limitations and execution brittleness: The system heavily depends on the quality of depth sensing and back-projection for 3D execution. In scenes with reflective surfaces, thin geometry, or heavy occlusion, 2D trace back-projection is prone to severe depth discontinuities, which is neither analyzed nor ablated in the paper.
